title: Refactoring with all five principles
idea: A SOLID refactor finds where a class keeps changing, then applies only the principle that moves each change into its own small, replaceable piece.
points: Start from real change requests, not from the list of five principles.
One god class usually breaks SRP, OCP and DIP at once; fix them together.
Refactor in small, behaviour-preserving steps, running the same output check after each.
Stop when every expected change touches one class; more splitting is overkill.

hero.title: From god class to plug-in parts

items.label: Map the change axes
items.text: List who asks for changes: new formats, new data sources, new upload targets.

items.label: SRP: split by job
items.text: Separate loading, rendering and delivery. `ExportJob` keeps only the order of steps.

items.label: OCP: formats as classes
items.text: Replace the `if` chain with `ExportFormat`. A new format is a new class.

items.label: LSP: honour the contract
items.text: Every format returns text for valid orders and never throws unexpectedly.

items.label: ISP: narrow ports
items.text: `Destination` has one method, so a test fake or an S3 adapter is tiny.

items.label: DIP: inject the details
items.text: The job receives source, format and destination; `main` decides which ones.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: `OrderExportJob` loads, formats and uploads in one method. Each change edits it, and a bug hides inside.

walk.text: SRP and DIP break here: the data is hard-wired into the job, so tests cannot replace it.
OCP breaks: formats live in an `if` chain that every new format must edit.
Tangled string building drops `cents` and leaves a trailing comma: the JSON is broken.
An unknown format fails only at runtime, after callers already depend on strings.
DIP breaks again: the job calls `new FtpUploader()`, welding policy to transport.
Run all three formats and compare the output with what a reader would expect.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Same feature, split into ports and plug-ins. Each principle names a line you can point to in an interview.

walk.text: `Order` is a validated record instead of a loose `String[]` row.
Two one-method ports, owned by the job. Lambdas or adapters can implement them.
`ExportFormat` is the extension point. Its comment states the contract every format must keep.
Each format is its own class. The JSON fixes are a separate, deliberate step after the split.
`ExportJob` validates its parts and only sequences load, render and put.
`main` wires concrete pieces. Adding XML means one new class plus one list entry.

pitfalls: Refactoring without a before-and-after output check silently changes behaviour; capture output first.
Adding interfaces for code nobody changes or tests creates indirection without payoff.
Mixing structure changes and bug fixes in one step hides which one changed the output.

quiz.q: A 40-line script exports one fixed CSV, once, with one owner. What should you do?
options: Split it into ports and adapters right away
Add an `ExportFormat` interface with one implementation
Move it into a Strategy pattern with a factory
Keep it; refactor when a second format or owner appears
quiz.why: SOLID pays off when change arrives. With one format, one owner and no tests needing seams, extra interfaces add indirection and no benefit.

takeaway: Refactor toward the changes you see, then stop.
